first.rationale: The two measured declines this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly addresses both. memory_86 and memory_31 both point at onboarding/signup friction, and memory_31 specifically reports a durable (not just immediate) activation lift, which matches the objective of sustainable qualified revenue. I verify exactly those two because they are the load-bearing evidence for the action I intend to take, and they are old (day 12 and day 52) relative to a market that has since shifted; I want to confirm the original records actually measured durable activation rather than a one-week bump, and confirm the segment they applied to. Promotional pricing is the obvious reflex against the competitor's entry pricing, but memory_73 explicitly says it damaged 30-day retention and should not be generalized -- taking that slot would likely buy acquisition against the primary objective. Referral incentives (memory_57) are clean but address neither observed decline. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is sound but is a different funnel and does not touch the SMB pressure or the activation drop. Activation messaging (memory_91) is the runner-up and stays queued if verification undercuts the onboarding memories. Downstream risk flagged: cutting required signup fields can degrade lead qualification and routing data, which can quietly reduce revenue quality even while activation metrics rise -- so the experiment must track qualified-revenue-per-signup and 30-day retention, not just completion and first-week activation. Uncertainty preserved: the inherited results predate the competitor's launch, so prior effect sizes may not transfer; I am running a standard experiment with a control rather than a broad rollout, and I will not overwrite the inherited memories with this quarter's result if the segments differ.

mid.rationale: Verification confirmed both onboarding memories and, importantly, differentiated them. exp_86 (flow shortening) is the cleaner instrument: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% -- it improves the metric that is actually down (-4% onboarding completion) while moving retention in the right direction, which is exactly what a sustainable-qualified-revenue objective wants. exp_31 (signup field-cutting) is real but weaker on the dimension I care about: retention -1%, qualified revenue only +4%, and explicitly SMB-only with no replication on other segments. So I take the slot for onboarding but scope the treatment to flow shortening / sequencing, not to stripping required signup fields. That scoping also retires most of the lead-quality concern I flagged earlier, since exp_86 did not achieve its lift by removing qualification data. I keep the flag active anyway because implementers routinely blur 'shorten onboarding' into 'remove fields,' and because exp_86 reported no qualified-revenue figure at all -- completion and retention improved, but revenue quality was simply not measured, so I will instrument qualified-revenue-per-signup and 30-day retention as guardrails rather than assume they follow. Onboarding is also upstream of the -6% activation drop, so this is the single action with a plausible path to both declines; activation_messaging (memory_91) remains the queued follow-up if the funnel data shows the loss is post-onboarding rather than during it. I continue to decline promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 is explicit that it damaged 30-day retention and should not be generalized, and buying price-sensitive SMB accounts that churn is a direct trade against the primary objective. Uncertainty preserved: all of this evidence predates the competitor launch (days 12 and 52 vs. day 76), so the market that produced these effect sizes no longer exists in the same form -- I run a controlled standard experiment, not a broad rollout, and I will record this cycle's result as a separate observation rather than overwriting exp_86 or exp_31, since a different competitive environment and a possibly different segment mix mean a divergent result would not falsify the originals.

final2.rationale: I am holding the decision. The competitor's second cut changes the urgency and the political temperature, but it does not add evidence about what works -- and the one slot has to be spent on the action with the best expected effect on sustainable qualified revenue, not the one that most visibly answers the news. Note the shape of the problem: doubled churn conversations are a retention event. memory_73's verified failure mode is precisely retention (materially reduced 30-day retention), with its upside on acquisition and headline revenue. Reaching for promotional pricing here would apply an acquisition instrument to a retention problem, using the exact lever whose archived record warns against generalizing it, and would likely convert a price-sensitive cohort into a discounted cohort that still churns -- worse, it resets the price anchor for that base permanently, which is hard to walk back next quarter. It also cannot win: we cannot out-cut a competitor whose strategy is entry pricing, and matching invites a third cut. By contrast exp_86 is verified at completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% -- it is the only lever I have with a measured positive retention effect, it targets the -4% completion and (upstream) the -6% activation declines, and faster time-to-value is the substantive answer to a price argument: accounts that reach value quickly are the ones least likely to leave over price. Scope stays flow-shortening, not signup field-cutting (exp_31 showed retention -1%, SMB-only, qualified revenue only +4%). Downstream risk still flagged: exp_86 never measured qualified revenue, so I instrument qualified-revenue-per-signup and 30-day retention as guardrails, and I want the SMB churn conversations tracked separately so we learn whether the losses are genuinely price-driven or value-realization-driven -- that distinction should drive next cycle's slot. Uncertainty preserved and now higher than on day 76: every inherited record predates both price cuts, so prior effect sizes may not transfer to a market where SMB switching costs have effectively dropped. That is an argument for a controlled standard experiment with a clean holdout, not for a broad rollout and not for abandoning the plan mid-cycle. I will log this cycle as a separate observation under changed competitive conditions rather than overwriting exp_86. Two things I am explicitly not claiming: that pricing is never the right response -- if next week's data shows churn is genuinely price-elastic rather than value-driven, a narrowly targeted, time-boxed, retention-instrumented offer to identified at-risk accounts is the candidate, and memory_57 (referral incentives, no measured retention harm) is the cleaner revenue lever to pair with it; and that holding is costless -- if leadership needs a same-day action, the non-experimental response is direct outreach and retention conversations with the named at-risk accounts, which does not consume the experiment slot.
